subChunks.title: useEffect: Side Effects and the Outside World
subChunks.hookHtml: Components render UI from data. But what about operations that reach outside the component — fetching from an API, reading localStorage, starting a timer, subscribing to a WebSocket? These are side effects: actions that touch the world beyond React's render cycle. useEffect is the hook that manages them safely.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is a side effect?

A side effect is anything a component does that isn't "take props and state → return JSX". Examples:

  • Fetching data from an API
  • Setting the document title
  • Starting or stopping a timer
  • Subscribing to a WebSocket or event listener
  • Reading/writing localStorage

Side effects don't belong directly in the render function — they run on every render, including intermediate ones, causing duplicated calls or infinite loops.

useEffect syntax

import { useEffect } from 'react';

useEffect(() => {
  // Side effect code goes here
}, [dependencies]);

useEffect takes two arguments: an effect function and a dependency array.

The dependency array — the most important part

// 1. No array — runs after EVERY render (rarely what you want):
useEffect(() => {
  console.log('Runs after every render');
});

// 2. Empty array — runs ONCE after the first render (mount):
useEffect(() => {
  console.log('Runs once on mount');
}, []);

// 3. With dependencies — runs after mount AND whenever a dep changes:
useEffect(() => {
  console.log('userId changed:', userId);
}, [userId]);

Vex: "The dependency array is a contract: 'this effect depends on these values.' If you use a value inside the effect, it must be in the array. ESLint's exhaustive-deps rule enforces this. If you find yourself wanting to omit a dependency to 'avoid re-running', that's a design smell — you probably need a different structure."

Cleanup functions

If your effect sets up a subscription or timer, it must tear it down when the component unmounts (or before the next run). Return a cleanup function:

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    setTick(t => t + 1);
  }, 1000);

  // This runs when the component unmounts or before the next effect:
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []); // Empty array: start once, clear on unmount

Without cleanup, the interval would keep running after the component unmounts — causing state updates on an unmounted component (a React warning) and eventually a memory leak.

Setting the document title — a safe first effect

function QuestPage({ questTitle }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    document.title = `${questTitle} — Arcane Academy`;

    // Optional cleanup: reset title when component unmounts
    return () => {
      document.title = 'Arcane Academy';
    };
  }, [questTitle]); // Re-run whenever questTitle changes

  return <h1>{questTitle}</h1>;
}

What useEffect is not for

Don't use useEffect to transform data for rendering — do that inline in the component body or with useMemo:

// ❌ Unnecessary effect — this is just a derived value:
const [filtered, setFiltered] = useState([]);
useEffect(() => {
  setFiltered(items.filter(i => i.done));
}, [items]);

// ✅ Compute it directly — no effect needed:
const filtered = items.filter(i => i.done);

storyBeats.text: Vex holds up a component diagram. Inside the render box, everything is clean. Outside it: timers, network requests, browser APIs. She draws a boundary between them.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: A component's render function must be pure — the same props and state always produce the same JSX. Fetching data, setting timers, reading localStorage — these are side effects. They touch the world outside React. useEffect is the designated place to run them safely, after the render is committed to the screen.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The dependency array is the key. Empty array: run once on mount. No array: run after every render. Values in the array: run after mount and whenever those values change. If you use a value inside the effect, it belongs in the array — no exceptions.

storyBeats.speaker: Effect with cleanup

Also render the title in an <h1 data-testid="heading"> so it is visible on screen.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <CountdownTimer seconds /> component from scratch. It takes a seconds prop (initial countdown value). Every second, the displayed count decreases by 1. When it reaches 0, display Time's up! instead of a number. Use useEffect for the interval and make sure you clean it up. Hint: you'll need both useState and useEffect.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain useEffect's dependency array to a colleague. What does it control? What are the three different behaviours depending on whether the array is absent, empty, or contains values? What breaks when you use a value inside an effect but leave it out of the dependency array?

questions.prompt: What does passing an empty array `[]` as useEffect's second argument cause?
options: The effect runs once after the first render and never again
The effect runs after every render
The effect never runs
The effect runs before the first render
questions.answer: The effect runs once after the first render and never again
questions.explanation: An empty dependency array tells React 'this effect has no dependencies — nothing can cause it to re-run.' It fires once after the initial render (mount) and the cleanup runs once when the component unmounts. This is the correct pattern for one-time setup like subscribing to a WebSocket or fetching initial data.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the function returned from a useEffect callback?
options: It runs when the component unmounts or before the next effect run — used to cancel subscriptions and clear timers
It runs before the effect to set up preconditions
It is a callback React calls with the effect's result
It tells React whether to re-run the effect
questions.answer: It runs when the component unmounts or before the next effect run — used to cancel subscriptions and clear timers
questions.explanation: The cleanup function prevents memory leaks and stale subscriptions. React calls it in two situations: when the component unmounts, and before re-running the effect (if dependencies changed). Always return a cleanup from effects that set up subscriptions, intervals, or event listeners.

options: [userId] — the effect must re-run whenever userId changes
[] — fetch only once on mount
No array — re-fetch on every render
[userId, fetchUser] — include all referenced values
questions.answer: [userId] — the effect must re-run whenever userId changes
questions.explanation: The effect uses userId, so it belongs in the dependency array. Without it, the effect would only run on mount and the displayed user would never update when userId changes. fetchUser is typically a stable function defined outside the component and doesn't need to be listed (or you can wrap it in useCallback if it's defined inside).

options: It creates an unnecessary extra render — filtered is a derived value that can be computed directly in the component body
useEffect cannot call setState functions
The filter function mutates the original array
Missing cleanup will cause a memory leak
questions.answer: It creates an unnecessary extra render — filtered is a derived value that can be computed directly in the component body
questions.explanation: Storing derived data in state (values computed from other state/props) adds a wasted render cycle: items changes → effect runs → setFiltered → another render. Instead, compute inline: const filtered = items.filter(i => i.done). This is synchronous, always up-to-date, and requires no effect.

subChunks.title: Fetching Data from APIs
subChunks.hookHtml: Most real React apps consume data from a server. Fetching, tracking loading state, handling errors, and displaying the result are the four-step pattern every component that talks to an API must implement. Get this pattern right once and you'll use it everywhere.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The three-state pattern

Every data fetch has three possible states your UI must handle:

  • Loading — the request is in flight
  • Error — the request failed
  • Success — data is available
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    setLoading(true);
    setError(null);

    fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${userId}`)
      .then(res => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return res.json();
      })
      .then(data => {
        setUser(data);
        setLoading(false);
      })
      .catch(err => {
        setError(err.message);
        setLoading(false);
      });
  }, [userId]);

  if (loading) return <p data-testid="loading">Loading...</p>;
  if (error)   return <p data-testid="error">Error: {error}</p>;
  return <div data-testid="user"><h2>{user.name}</h2></div>;
}

Using async/await with useEffect

You cannot make the effect callback itself async (it would return a Promise, which React doesn't expect). Define an async function inside the effect and call it immediately:

useEffect(() => {
  async function loadUser() {
    try {
      setLoading(true);
      const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`);
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      const data = await res.json();
      setUser(data);
    } catch (err) {
      setError(err.message);
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  }

  loadUser();
}, [userId]);

Avoiding race conditions with a cleanup flag

If the user changes userId quickly, two requests may be in flight simultaneously. The slower one might resolve last and overwrite the correct data. A cleanup flag prevents stale updates:

useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;

  async function loadUser() {
    try {
      setLoading(true);
      const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`);
      const data = await res.json();
      if (!cancelled) setUser(data); // Only update if still current
    } catch (err) {
      if (!cancelled) setError(err.message);
    } finally {
      if (!cancelled) setLoading(false);
    }
  }

  loadUser();
  return () => { cancelled = true; }; // Cleanup: mark as stale
}, [userId]);

Vex: "Always reset loading and error state at the start of a new fetch. If you skip resetting error, a user who retried after an error will see the old error flash briefly before the new data arrives. Small detail. Visible to every user."

Using a public test API

For practice, jsonplaceholder.typicode.com provides free REST endpoints with realistic fake data:

// GET /posts — array of 100 posts
// GET /posts/1 — single post
// GET /users — array of 10 users
fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1')
  .then(r => r.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data));
// { id: 1, title: '...', body: '...', userId: 1 }

storyBeats.text: A messenger raven arrives with a scroll. Vex holds it up: 'The Guild's quest board is now live — data from a real server. How do we display it?'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Every data fetch has three possible states: loading, error, and success. Your UI must handle all three. Show a spinner while loading. Show an error message if the request fails. Show the data when it arrives. Skip any of the three and users will see broken, confusing interfaces.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The effect can't be async directly — React doesn't expect a Promise back. Define an async function inside the effect and call it immediately. This is the standard pattern. You'll write it dozens of times.

storyBeats.speaker: The three-state fetch pattern

  • On error: render <p data-testid="error">Failed to load post.</p>

Show a loading state, an error state, and — on success — render each user's name and email in a list. Include a Retry button that appears in the error state and re-triggers the fetch when clicked. subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the three-state data-fetching pattern. What state variables do you need, what are their initial values, and why? What breaks if you forget to reset the error state before re-fetching? What is a race condition in this context, and how does a cleanup flag prevent it?

questions.prompt: Why can't you make the useEffect callback itself an async function?
options: An async function returns a Promise, but useEffect expects either nothing or a cleanup function
async/await is not supported inside React hooks
It would cause the component to suspend rendering
Async callbacks are not supported in JavaScript functions
questions.answer: An async function returns a Promise, but useEffect expects either nothing or a cleanup function
questions.explanation: useEffect's return value is treated as a cleanup function. If you return a Promise (by making the effect async), React doesn't know how to call it as a cleanup, and you'll get unexpected behavior. The fix: define an async function inside the effect and call it immediately — the effect itself remains synchronous.

questions.prompt: The Fetch API does not throw an error for 4xx or 5xx HTTP responses. How do you handle this?
options: Check `res.ok` and throw manually: `if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status)`
The fetch Promise rejects automatically for any non-2xx response
Use res.status === 200 to check before calling res.json()
Wrap the entire fetch in a try/catch — it will catch HTTP errors automatically
questions.answer: Check `res.ok` and throw manually: `if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status)`
questions.explanation: fetch() only rejects its Promise for network failures (no connection, DNS failure). A 404 or 500 response resolves successfully with res.ok === false. You must check res.ok and throw to route those cases into your catch block. This is one of the most common data-fetching bugs.

questions.prompt: After a failed fetch, the user clicks a button to retry. They see the old error flash before the new loading state appears. What is the most likely cause?
options: The error state is not reset at the start of the new fetch
setLoading(true) is called before setError(null)
The retry button is rendering a new component instance
React batches the state updates and applies loading last
questions.answer: The error state is not reset at the start of the new fetch
questions.explanation: If you set loading to true but don't clear the error, the component first renders with loading=true AND error='...' — whichever branch runs first shows stale UI. Always reset both at the start of every fetch: setLoading(true); setError(null).

questions.prompt: A user quickly switches between two userId values (1, then 2). Without a cleanup flag, what can go wrong?
options: Both requests complete, but the slower one may resolve last and overwrite the result for userId=2 with data for userId=1
React cancels the first fetch automatically when userId changes
The component will throw a runtime error due to two concurrent state updates
Both results are displayed simultaneously, causing a duplicate render
questions.answer: Both requests complete, but the slower one may resolve last and overwrite the result for userId=2 with data for userId=1
questions.explanation: This is a race condition. Two fetches are in flight; the network doesn't guarantee order. If the fetch for userId=1 is slower, it resolves after userId=2's fetch, calling setUser with stale data. The cleanup flag (let cancelled = true in cleanup) prevents the stale response from calling setState.

subChunks.title: React Router: Navigation and URL Params
subChunks.hookHtml: Single-page apps don't reload the page when navigating — they swap components. React Router gives your app URL-based navigation: different URLs render different components, the back button works, and links are shareable. It's the difference between an app and a demo.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Setup — wrapping your app in a Router

// main.jsx
import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router-dom';
import App from './App';

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <App />
  </BrowserRouter>
);

BrowserRouter provides the routing context for the entire app. It must wrap everything that uses Router features.

Defining routes

import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<HomePage />} />
      <Route path="/quests" element={<QuestListPage />} />
      <Route path="/quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />
      <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} />
    </Routes>
  );
}

:id is a URL parameter — a dynamic segment captured from the URL. * is a catch-all for unknown routes.

Navigation — Link and useNavigate

import { Link, useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';

// Declarative navigation — use in JSX:
<Link to="/quests">View Quests</Link>
<Link to={`/quests/${quest.id}`}>{quest.title}</Link>

// Programmatic navigation — use after an action:
function QuestForm() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();

  async function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    await submitQuest(formData);
    navigate('/quests'); // Redirect after success
  }
}

Always use <Link> instead of <a href> for internal navigation. <a> triggers a full page reload; <Link> uses the Router's client-side navigation.

Reading URL parameters

import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom';

// Route: /quests/:id
function QuestDetailPage() {
  const { id } = useParams(); // id is always a string — parse if needed
  const questId = parseInt(id, 10);

  // ... fetch quest by questId
}

Nested routes and shared layouts

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<Layout />}>
        <!-- Child routes render inside <Outlet /> in Layout -->
        <Route index element={<HomePage />} />
        <Route path="quests" element={<QuestListPage />} />
        <Route path="quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />
      </Route>
    </Routes>
  );
}

// Layout renders the nav bar + current child page:
import { Outlet } from 'react-router-dom';
function Layout() {
  return (
    <>
      <nav><Link to="/">Home</Link> | <Link to="/quests">Quests</Link></nav>
      <main><Outlet /></main>
    </>
  );
}

Vex: "The Outlet component is where React Router renders the matched child route inside a layout. Think of it as a placeholder that says 'put the current page's content here.' Without an Outlet, nested child routes never appear."

storyBeats.text: The single-page workbench now has multiple rooms — different views accessible through doorways. Vex gestures at the doorways.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: A real app has multiple pages. React Router gives URLs meaning without reloading the page. Different URLs render different components. The back button works. Links can be bookmarked and shared. Without routing, you have a demo. With routing, you have an app.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Three concepts to master: Routes (which component to show at which URL), Link (navigate without a page reload), and useParams (read the dynamic segments from the URL). The fourth — useNavigate — is for redirecting after actions like form submissions.

storyBeats.speaker: Routes, Link, and useParams

  • About page (/about): renders <h1 data-testid="about">About</h1> and a <Link to="/">Home</Link>

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Build a mini quest browser from scratch with three pages:

  • / — lists three quests (hardcoded) as Links to /quests/1, /quests/2, /quests/3
  • /quests/:id — shows the quest ID from the URL in a heading: Quest #1

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between using an `<a href>` tag and React Router's `<Link>` component for internal navigation. What does each do to the browser? When would you use `useNavigate` instead of `<Link>`?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between using `<a href="/about">` and `<Link to="/about">` inside a React Router app?
options: <a> causes a full page reload; <Link> uses client-side navigation without reloading
They are functionally identical — React Router intercepts all <a> tags
<Link> is slower because it re-renders the entire app on navigation
<a> is required for accessibility; <Link> should only be used for buttons
questions.answer: <a> causes a full page reload; <Link> uses client-side navigation without reloading
questions.explanation: A standard <a href> makes the browser request a new URL and reload the entire page — losing React state and showing a flash of white. React Router's <Link> pushes to the browser's history API without a page reload, React swaps the matching component, and state persists. Always use <Link> for internal navigation.

questions.prompt: The route `/quests/:id` is matched. Inside the `QuestDetailPage` component, how do you access the `id` value?
options: const { id } = useParams()
const id = props.params.id
const id = useRoute().id
const { id } = useLocation().state
questions.answer: const { id } = useParams()
questions.explanation: useParams() returns an object containing all dynamic segments from the matched URL. For a route /quests/:id matched against /quests/42, useParams() returns { id: '42' }. Note that URL params are always strings — parse to a number if needed.

questions.prompt: After a form submission succeeds, you want to redirect the user to `/dashboard`. Which React Router tool do you use?
options: useNavigate — call navigate('/dashboard') in the submit handler after the async action succeeds
Link — render <Link to="/dashboard" /> in the form's onSubmit
useLocation — update the current location object
Route — add a redirect Route that activates on form success
questions.answer: useNavigate — call navigate('/dashboard') in the submit handler after the async action succeeds
questions.explanation: Link is for declarative navigation in JSX — clicking an element. useNavigate is for programmatic navigation triggered by code: after a successful API call, after a timeout, or after any event that isn't a direct user click on a link. Call the returned navigate function with the target path.

questions.prompt: You have a Layout component with a nav bar that should appear on every page. The page content should render below it. Which React Router feature renders the matched child route inside the Layout?
options: <Outlet /> — a placeholder component from react-router-dom that renders the current child route
props.children — pass the current page as children to Layout
<Route /> — nest a Route inside Layout's JSX
useLocation() — read the current path and conditionally render the right component
questions.answer: <Outlet /> — a placeholder component from react-router-dom that renders the current child route
questions.explanation: When you use nested routes (<Route element={<Layout />}> with child <Route> elements inside), React Router renders Layout's element and replaces <Outlet /> with the matched child route's element. This is how you share a nav bar, sidebar, or page frame across multiple routes without duplicating it.

subChunks.title: Forms: Validation and Multi-Field Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: Single-field forms are straightforward. Real forms have five, ten, twenty fields — and they need validation, error messages, and submission state. The patterns you use for multi-field forms determine whether your code stays manageable or collapses under its own weight.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Managing multi-field state with an object

Instead of a separate useState for every field, store all field values in one object:

function RegistrationForm() {
  const [fields, setFields] = useState({
    username: '',
    email: '',
    password: '',
  });

  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, value } = e.target;
    setFields(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value }));
  }

  return (
    <form>
      <input name="username" value={fields.username} onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="email"    value={fields.email}    onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="password" value={fields.password} onChange={handleChange} type="password" />
    </form>
  );
}

The trick: name attribute on each input matches the key in the state object. One handleChange function handles all fields using computed property names ([name]: value).

Validation — two strategies

Validate on submit: Check all fields when the user submits. Simple, less annoying for users.

const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

function validate(fields) {
  const errs = {};
  if (!fields.username.trim()) errs.username = 'Username is required';
  if (!fields.email.includes('@')) errs.email = 'Enter a valid email';
  if (fields.password.length < 8) errs.password = 'At least 8 characters';
  return errs;
}

function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const errs = validate(fields);
  if (Object.keys(errs).length > 0) {
    setErrors(errs);
    return;
  }
  // Proceed with submission
}

Validate on blur: Validate a field when the user leaves it (onBlur). More immediate feedback.

function handleBlur(e) {
  const { name, value } = e.target;
  // Validate just this field and merge into errors:
  const fieldError = validateField(name, value);
  setErrors(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: fieldError }));
}

Submission state

Prevent double-submissions and show feedback during async operations:

const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
const [submitError, setSubmitError] = useState(null);

async function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  if (submitting) return; // Guard against double-click

  setSubmitting(true);
  setSubmitError(null);

  try {
    await registerUser(fields);
    navigate('/welcome');
  } catch (err) {
    setSubmitError(err.message);
  } finally {
    setSubmitting(false);
  }
}

// In JSX:
<button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>
  {submitting ? 'Creating account...' : 'Create Account'}
</button>

Vex: "Disable the submit button while submitting. Show loading text. These are not polish — they are correctness. A double-submitted registration creates two accounts. A form that shows no feedback while waiting looks broken. Both cost you users."

useRef for uncontrolled inputs

For simple cases where you only need the value on submit (not on every keystroke), an uncontrolled input with a ref is lighter:

import { useRef } from 'react';

function SimpleSearch() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    console.log(inputRef.current.value);
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input ref={inputRef} type="text" />
      <button type="submit">Search</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Prefer controlled inputs (useState) for most forms — they are easier to validate, reset, and test. Use useRef for cases where you truly only need the value at submission time and have no need for real-time validation.

storyBeats.text: A complex registration scroll appears on the workbench — username, email, password, repeat password, role selection. Vex spreads it flat.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: One useState per field is fine for two fields. For ten fields it is noise. Store all field values in one state object — the field's name attribute is the key. One handleChange function updates any field by reading e.target.name.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Validation and submission state are the parts beginners skip. Validate on submit at minimum — build an errors object, set it in state, show the messages inline. Disable the submit button while the async call is in flight. Both of these are correctness, not polish.

storyBeats.speaker: One handleChange for all fields

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <LoginForm onSubmit /> component with two fields: email and password.

  • Use a single state object for both fields and a single handleChange handler
  • On submit, validate: email must contain @, password must be at least 6 characters
  • Show inline errors in <p data-testid="error-email"> and <p data-testid="error-password"> when invalid
  • If valid, call onSubmit(fields) and do not show errors
  • Disable the submit button while submitting state is true (you can simulate this with a 1-second delay)

guidedPracticeTests.label: Shows password error when too short

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <RegistrationForm> from scratch with three fields: username (required, min 3 chars), email (must contain @), password (min 8 chars). Use a single state object and a single handleChange. Show inline validation errors. Disable the submit button while submitting. On successful validation, log the fields to the console. No scaffold.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the pattern of storing all form fields in one state object with a shared handleChange function. Why is this preferable to a separate useState for each field? Walk through what happens step by step when a user types into the email input.

questions.prompt: In the single-object form state pattern, how does one `handleChange` function update the correct field for any input?
options: It reads `e.target.name` (matching the input's `name` attribute) and uses it as a computed property key to update only that field
It reads `e.target.id` and finds the matching state key by ID
React automatically maps onChange events to the matching state key by input position
It updates all fields simultaneously and React diffs to find the changed one
questions.answer: It reads `e.target.name` (matching the input's `name` attribute) and uses it as a computed property key to update only that field
questions.explanation: const { name, value } = e.target gives you the input's name attribute and its new value. setFields(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value })) spreads the existing fields and overwrites only the matching key. This works for any number of fields as long as each input's name attribute matches the corresponding state key.

questions.prompt: Why should the submit button be disabled while a form submission is in progress?
options: To prevent double-submissions — a second click would trigger a second async request before the first completes
Disabled buttons look more professional in loading states
React throws an error if state is updated on an unmounted component after double-submit
The browser would reload the page if a submit event fires twice
questions.answer: To prevent double-submissions — a second click would trigger a second async request before the first completes
questions.explanation: If the user clicks Submit twice before the async request completes, two identical requests go out. For actions like creating an account or placing an order, this creates duplicate records. Disabling the button (and optionally checking a submitting guard inside handleSubmit) prevents this class of bug.

questions.prompt: When is `useRef` for an uncontrolled input preferable over `useState` for a controlled input?
options: When you only need the value at submission time and have no real-time validation, character counting, or derived UI
When the form has more than 5 fields — useRef performs better at scale
When the input value might be empty — useState can't represent empty strings
useRef is always preferable — controlled inputs cause unnecessary re-renders
questions.answer: When you only need the value at submission time and have no real-time validation, character counting, or derived UI
questions.explanation: Controlled inputs re-render on every keystroke — which is exactly what you need for live validation or character counters. If you don't need any of that (e.g., a simple search box that only needs the value on Enter), useRef reads the value once at submission without any state overhead. Most forms benefit from controlled inputs.

questions.prompt: Validate-on-submit vs validate-on-blur: which strategy is more appropriate for a long registration form?
options: Validate on blur for individual fields (immediate per-field feedback) combined with a full validate-on-submit pass as the final gate
Validate on submit only — validation on blur is too aggressive and frustrates users
Validate on every keystroke using onChange — gives the most immediate feedback
Validate on blur only — on-submit validation is redundant if each field was already validated
questions.answer: Validate on blur for individual fields (immediate per-field feedback) combined with a full validate-on-submit pass as the final gate
questions.explanation: Validating on every keystroke (onChange) shows errors while the user is still typing — e.g., 'email is invalid' appearing after the first character. Blur validation shows errors after the user finishes a field, which feels natural. A final on-submit pass catches fields the user skipped entirely. The combination gives good UX without being aggressive.

subChunks.title: Component Patterns: Composition and Lifting State
subChunks.hookHtml: As apps grow, two problems emerge: state that needs to be shared between components, and UI that needs to be flexible without becoming a tangle of props. Lifting state and composition patterns are the structural answers — and getting them right is what separates scalable React apps from spaghetti.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Lifting state up

When two components need to share the same state, move the state to their closest common ancestor and pass it down as props:

// ❌ Each input owns its own state — they can't see each other:
function FilterInput() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  // List doesn't know about query
}

// ✅ Parent owns the state and distributes it:
function SearchPage() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');

  return (
    <>
      <FilterInput query={query} onQueryChange={setQuery} />
      <ResultsList query={query} />
    </>
  );
}

function FilterInput({ query, onQueryChange }) {
  return (
    <input value={query} onChange={(e) => onQueryChange(e.target.value)} />
  );
}

Prop drilling — and when it becomes a problem

Passing props through two or three levels is fine. When you're passing the same prop through five levels of components that don't use it themselves — just to get it to a deeply nested component — that's prop drilling. Solutions:

  • Component composition (see below) — often eliminates the need to drill
  • Context API — for truly global data (covered in Expert tier)

Composition: children and render slots

Instead of passing data down through many levels, rearrange the component tree so the component that needs the data is rendered at the right level:

// ❌ Prop drilling: App → Page → Section → Widget → Button needs user
function App() {
  const user = useUser();
  return <Page user={user} />;
}
function Page({ user }) {
  return <Section user={user} />;  // Page doesn't use user itself
}

// ✅ Composition: render <UserButton> at the level that has user
function App() {
  const user = useUser();
  return (
    <Page>
      <Section>
        <UserButton user={user} />  {/* user only travels one level */}
      </Section>
    </Page>
  );
}
function Page({ children }) { return <div>{children}</div>; }
function Section({ children }) { return <section>{children}</section>; }

The render prop pattern

Pass a function as a prop that returns JSX — gives the parent control over what renders, the child control over when it renders:

function DataLoader({ url, render }) {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  useEffect(() => { fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(setData); }, [url]);
  if (!data) return <p>Loading...</p>;
  return render(data); // Parent decides how to display it
}

// Usage:
<DataLoader
  url="/api/user"
  render={(user) => <UserProfile name={user.name} />}
/>

Vex: "Render props look clever and they are sometimes the right tool. But before reaching for them, ask: can I solve this with lifting state and children props? Usually the answer is yes, and the result is simpler."

Controlled components — the React way

A controlled component pattern applies beyond inputs. Any component whose state is owned externally and passed in as props is 'controlled':

// Uncontrolled modal — owns its own open/closed state
function Modal() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
}

// Controlled modal — parent owns the state, gives full control:
function Modal({ open, onClose }) {
  if (!open) return null;
  return <div className="modal">... <button onClick={onClose}>Close</button></div>;
}

Controlled components are more reusable — the parent can open/close the modal in response to anything, not just clicks inside the modal itself.

storyBeats.text: Two components on the workbench need to stay in sync — a search input and a results list. Neither can see the other's state. Vex draws an arrow pointing up to their parent.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: When two components need the same data, don't try to sync them — lift the state to their common parent and pass it down. The parent owns truth. Children receive and report. This is the first structural pattern every React developer must master.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Prop drilling becomes a problem at depth — passing props through components that don't use them, just to get data somewhere deep. Before reaching for Context, ask: can composition solve this? Passing children or rendering components higher in the tree often cuts the chain entirely.

storyBeats.speaker: Lifting state to the common parent

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <FilterableList> component that lifts state correctly:

  • It contains a <SearchInput value onSearch /> and an <ItemList items />
  • The parent <FilterableList> owns the query state and passes it to both children
  • SearchInput renders a controlled text input and calls onSearch with the input value on each keystroke
  • ItemList receives the full items array (objects with id and name) and renders only items whose name includes the query (case-insensitive)
  • Show <p data-testid="empty">No results.</p> when nothing matches

guidedPracticeTests.label: Shows empty state when no match

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a controlled accordion from scratch. An <Accordion> component renders a list of items (each with a title and content). Only one item can be expanded at a time. The expanded item's index is owned by the Accordion parent — each AccordionItem receives an isOpen boolean and an onToggle callback. No scaffold.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain 'lifting state up' to a colleague. What is the symptom that tells you state needs to be lifted? Walk through a concrete example — a filter input and a filtered list — describing exactly what changes when you lift the state.

questions.prompt: When should you lift state up to a parent component?
options: When two or more sibling components need to read or respond to the same state
When a component has too many useState calls and needs to simplify
When the state is only read once during the component's lifetime
Only when the component is re-rendering too frequently
questions.answer: When two or more sibling components need to read or respond to the same state
questions.explanation: State lives at the lowest level of the component tree where it needs to be accessible. If only one component needs it, keep it there. If two siblings need it, the closest common ancestor is the right home. 'Lifting state' means moving it up to that ancestor and distributing it via props.

questions.prompt: What is prop drilling and at what point does it become a problem?
options: Passing props through intermediate components that don't use the data themselves — it becomes a problem when the chain is 3-5+ levels deep
Passing too many props to a single component — more than 5 props is a code smell
Passing functions as props — this creates tight coupling between parent and child
Prop drilling is always a problem and should be avoided at any depth
questions.answer: Passing props through intermediate components that don't use the data themselves — it becomes a problem when the chain is 3-5+ levels deep
questions.explanation: Two or three levels of prop passing is normal and manageable. The problem appears when Page passes user to Section which passes it to Widget which passes it to Button — and none of the intermediate components use user themselves. Every added level couples more components to the data shape and makes refactoring harder.

questions.prompt: A Modal component that owns its open/closed state internally can only be opened by clicks inside itself. How do you make it openable from anywhere in the app?
options: Make it a controlled component: accept open and onClose as props, let the parent own the state
Use a global variable to store the modal's open state
Add a ref to the Modal and call modalRef.current.open() from outside
Use useEffect to watch for a custom DOM event and open on that
questions.answer: Make it a controlled component: accept open and onClose as props, let the parent own the state
questions.explanation: A controlled Modal receives its open state from outside and calls onClose when it wants to close. The parent can open it from a button, a timeout, or any event. The uncontrolled version (internal state) can only be opened by something inside the modal. Controlled components are more reusable and composable.

questions.prompt: Data is needed 5 levels deep in the component tree. Before reaching for Context API, which composition technique often eliminates the prop drilling?
options: Render the component that needs the data at the level where the data is available, and pass it as children down through layout components
Convert all intermediate components to class components to access the data via this.props
Use useRef to store the data at the top level and read it anywhere without props
Inline all intermediate components into one large parent component
questions.answer: Render the component that needs the data at the level where the data is available, and pass it as children down through layout components
questions.explanation: Component composition is the first tool to reach for before Context. If UserButton needs the user object that lives in App, render <UserButton user={user} /> in App and pass it as children through Page → Section → Widget. Page, Section, and Widget become layout-only components that don't need to know about user at all. The data travels one level, not five.

subChunks.title: Custom Hooks: Extracting Reusable Logic
subChunks.hookHtml: When the same combination of useState and useEffect appears in three components, it's time to extract a custom hook. Custom hooks let you package stateful logic — fetching, timers, local storage sync, form handling — into a single reusable function. The result: components that are readable, and logic that is testable.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is a custom hook?

A custom hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks. That's the entire definition.

// This is a custom hook:
function useWindowWidth() {
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth);

  useEffect(() => {
    const handleResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
    window.addEventListener('resize', handleResize);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', handleResize);
  }, []);

  return width;
}

// Used in any component:
function ResponsiveLayout() {
  const width = useWindowWidth();
  return <p>{width > 768 ? 'Desktop' : 'Mobile'}</p>;
}

The use prefix is a convention React enforces: hooks can only be called at the top level of components or other hooks. The prefix signals to React's linting tools where hook rules apply.

useFetch — the most useful custom hook you'll write

function useFetch(url) {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;

    async function load() {
      setLoading(true);
      setError(null);
      try {
        const res = await fetch(url);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        const json = await res.json();
        if (!cancelled) setData(json);
      } catch (e) {
        if (!cancelled) setError(e.message);
      } finally {
        if (!cancelled) setLoading(false);
      }
    }

    load();
    return () => { cancelled = true; };
  }, [url]);

  return { data, loading, error };
}

// Now every component that fetches data is a one-liner:
function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  const { data: user, loading, error } = useFetch(`/api/users/${userId}`);
  if (loading) return <p>Loading...</p>;
  if (error)   return <p>Error: {error}</p>;
  return <h2>{user.name}</h2>;
}

useLocalStorage

function useLocalStorage(key, initialValue) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(() => {
    try {
      const stored = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return stored ? JSON.parse(stored) : initialValue;
    } catch {
      return initialValue;
    }
  });

  function setStoredValue(newValue) {
    setValue(newValue);
    localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(newValue));
  }

  return [value, setStoredValue];
}

// Drop-in replacement for useState that persists across page reloads:
const [theme, setTheme] = useLocalStorage('theme', 'light');

When to extract a custom hook

Extract when:

  • The same useState + useEffect combination appears in multiple components
  • A component's logic is complex enough that the hook logic dominates — making the component hard to read
  • You want to unit test the logic independently of the UI

Don't extract when the logic is used in only one place and straightforward — premature extraction adds indirection without benefit.

Vex: "Custom hooks are the final piece of the Foundation-to-Practitioner bridge. Components describe what to render. Custom hooks contain how to get the data that drives the render. Keep them separate and both become easier to read, test, and change."

storyBeats.text: Three components on the workbench each contain the same fetch-loading-error pattern — copied and slightly modified each time. Vex circles all three.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: When you see the same useState and useEffect combination in three places, that is a custom hook waiting to be written. A custom hook is just a function that starts with 'use' and calls other hooks. Extract it once. Use it everywhere.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: useFetch is the first custom hook most developers write because it has the highest leverage — every component that loads data goes from 15 lines to 3. The hook contains all the complexity; the component contains only intent.

storyBeats.speaker: useFetch — write once, use everywhere

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Extract the data-fetching logic from the lesson into a useFetch(url) custom hook, then use it in a <QuestList> component.

  • useFetch accepts a URL string and returns { data, loading, error }
  • It handles loading state, error state, and the race-condition cleanup flag
  • QuestList calls useFetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos?_limit=5') and renders a loading message, error message, or a <ul> of item titles
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a useLocalStorage(key, initialValue) custom hook from scratch. It should behave exactly like useState — return [value, setValue] — but persist the value to localStorage under key on every update, and read the stored value as the initial value on mount. Then use it in a <ThemeToggle> component that persists 'light' or 'dark' across page refreshes. No scaffold.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a custom hook is and why the `use` prefix matters. Walk through how you would extract a repeated fetch pattern into a `useFetch` hook — what does the hook contain, what does it return, and what does the component look like after the extraction?

questions.prompt: What are the two requirements for a function to be a React custom hook?
options: Its name must start with `use`, and it must call at least one React hook
It must be defined inside a component and return JSX
It must accept props as its first argument and return state
It must be exported from a separate file and imported explicitly
questions.answer: Its name must start with `use`, and it must call at least one React hook
questions.explanation: The `use` prefix is a convention React's linter and runtime use to enforce hook rules (don't call hooks inside conditions or loops, don't call hooks outside components or other hooks). Any function starting with `use` that calls useState, useEffect, or other hooks is a valid custom hook.

questions.prompt: Two components that call the same custom hook — do they share state?
options: No — each component gets its own independent state from the hook
Yes — hooks share state between all components that call them
Only if the hook uses useContext internally
Only if both components are rendered by the same parent
questions.answer: No — each component gets its own independent state from the hook
questions.explanation: Custom hooks are not singletons. Each call to a custom hook creates an independent set of state variables and effects for that specific component instance. This is the same as calling useState directly — two components with useState(0) have two separate, independent values.

questions.prompt: You have a `useFetch(url)` hook. A component calls it with a URL that depends on a prop. What must you ensure about the URL argument?
options: The full URL string must be constructed before passing to useFetch, and the hook's dependency array must include url
Pass the base URL and params separately — useFetch builds the final URL internally
Memoize the URL with useMemo to prevent the effect from re-running
The URL must be a constant — dynamic URLs require a separate useEffect
questions.answer: The full URL string must be constructed before passing to useFetch, and the hook's dependency array must include url
questions.explanation: useFetch receives a url argument and uses it in its internal useEffect. That effect's dependency array must include url so the effect re-runs and re-fetches when the URL changes. The component is responsible for building the correct URL string before passing it: useFetch(`/api/users/${userId}`).

questions.prompt: When is it NOT appropriate to extract logic into a custom hook?
options: When the logic is used in only one place and is straightforward — the abstraction adds indirection without benefit
When the logic involves more than two useState calls
When the hook would need to call useEffect
When the logic is synchronous — custom hooks are for async operations only
questions.answer: When the logic is used in only one place and is straightforward — the abstraction adds indirection without benefit
questions.explanation: Extract when the pattern repeats across components or when a component's logic is complex enough that the hook dominates readability. Don't extract for the sake of 'cleanliness' when there's only one usage — you create an additional file to navigate, a new abstraction to understand, and no concrete benefit. Premature extraction is a real problem in React codebases.
